newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israeli PM says steeper budget cut may be needed.
newsitem.headline: Israeli PM says steeper budget cut may be needed.

text.p: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said on Thursday that he continues to back the 4.9 billion shekel spending cut planned for the 1997 budget and added that further reductions may be needed.
Defending the controversial cuts, Netanyahu blamed the previous Labour government for spending policies that "led us to a situation of lower savings, a wider deficit and rising interest rates".
"Now we have taken control of the wheel and are turning us back in the right direction," he said.
Speaking to a group of business leaders in Tel Aviv, he said the cuts were needed not because of unforseen rises in expenses but because of lower-than-projected revenues.
He said budgetary discipline was a key test of the government's performance on the economy.

The cabinet approved the 4.9 billion shekel cut, equal to 3.2 percent of 1997 spending, last July. But the plan remains controversial, even among the government's coalition partners, who say the cuts fall hardest on the poor.
The budget will be submitted to parliament with only cosmetic changes on October 29. Parliament has until the end of the year to approve the budget.
Finance Minister Dan Meridor also said this week that further spending cuts may be required in 1997.

Netanyahu promised that the government's long-awaited privatisation programme would be unveiled in November. He gave no indication of what the programme would entail, but suggested it might include the state-owned television and the banks.

Netanyahu said the government would also address the shortage of skilled labour for high technology. He noted that an interministerial committee had been formed recently to examine various proposals, among them re-training of immigrants.
The prime minister said Israel's heavy tax burden had caused many companies to move production out of the country to places where costs were lower.
